summary:
Martinique is an overseas department of France and stands under the French national framework: Article 73 of the Constitution applies French law to the department in full, so the substantive provisions a visitor would rely on — identity documents, criminal law, anti-discrimination and the marriage regime — are national law operating on the island.

Prison is the sharpest documented exposure for a trans visitor detained here. Martinique's correctional establishments are French prisons and stand under the same placement rule as the mainland: under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code, placement follows the gender marker on the detainee's identity documents rather than anatomy, which puts most trans women into all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them. Reporting from January 2018 records the threat in direct terms — 'we don't want any women here'.

The CGLPL, France's detention-places watchdog, issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 finding 'the persistence of serious violations' of the fundamental rights of transgender detainees across all French places of deprivation of liberty. It rests on referrals made since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people and on-site inspections in which eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed, and its recommendations cover placement, isolation, safety and staff training. As a finding on all French places of deprivation of liberty, it binds the department's establishments.

The Rights in Exile (AsyLex) resource page for Martinique gathers local support organisations, case law and country-of-origin experts alongside the provisions that apply on the island, giving a single point of entry for locally grounded legal material.

Community infrastructure exists and operates on the island. JM Concept 972 runs information, meetings and services for Martinique's LGBT community, and LGBTQ organisations listed for the overseas departments include AIDES Territoire Martinique, KAP Caraïbe, Tjenbé Rèd Prévention and SAFE SXM.
tangentialFactors:
The on-site evidence behind the CGLPL's 2021 opinion was gathered at four establishments of mainland France — Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse — and none in Martinique. The finding covers all French places of deprivation of liberty, but the inspections that produced it did not include the department's own facilities.

The Rights in Exile page is built for an asylum context. Its case law and country-of-origin experts are assembled to support claims by people seeking protection, which makes them a closer fit for someone in a removal or status procedure than for a short-term visitor weighing ordinary travel risk.

No trans-specific violence incident, prosecution or court decision on the island appears in the sources available for this entry, so the department's own enforcement picture cannot be compared with the mainland's documented record.
localsOnly:
JM Concept 972 is a Martinique lesbian, gay, bi and trans network providing information, meetings and services to the island's community, and it runs private parties and garden parties supported by gay-friendly heterosexual supporters. Events are listed for 4 July, 15 August and 5 September 2025, indicating active, dated operation rather than a dormant listing.

LGBTQ organisations listed for the overseas departments include AIDES Territoire Martinique, KAP Caraïbe, Tjenbé Rèd Prévention and SAFE SXM, giving residents local prevention and support contacts on the island and in the neighbouring islands.

The Rights in Exile (AsyLex) Martinique page lists local support organisations, case law and country-of-origin experts, which residents can use to identify practitioners familiar with the department's situation.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Martinique-specific enforcement or litigation record for the discrimination instruments that apply on the island is documented in the sources available for this entry; whether any complaint has been brought and how it was resolved is unresolved.

Whether the CGLPL's recommendations on placement, isolation, safety and staff training have been implemented in Martinique's own establishments is not sourced. The opinion states the national finding; it does not report on the department's facilities individually.

No Martinique-specific data on gender-affirming healthcare — waiting times on the island, availability of clinicians, uptake of the long-term-illness scheme — is documented here, so access cannot be assessed from this entry.

No trans-specific violence incident with a date and outcome is recorded for the island in the available sources. The absence of such a record is not evidence that none occurs.
